name: Google Maps Design System
summary: iOS design reference for Google Maps' map-first UI — pin colors, bottom sheet, and turn-by-turn typography for map-centric apps.
description: A structured reference distilled from Google Maps' iOS interface, covering its four-color pin system, floating search bar, bottom-sheet drawer, and navigation-mode type and motion, for use when designing or building a map-centric SwiftUI app.

whatYouGet: Full hex palette for the four Google-logo pin roles plus map-tile tones (roads, water, parks, buildings) in light and dark
A two-font type ramp (display face for headings/CTAs, a denser face for body and data) with exact sizes and weights per UI role
Component specs for the floating search bar, primary map action button, bottom-sheet drawer with detents, and turn-by-turn navigation cards
Motion and haptic timing for pin drops, sheet detent snapping, and the pulsing location indicator
A responsive and touch-target table spanning the smallest current iPhone through iPad
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in geospatial, map-first consumer apps. You have shipped production features that layer floating UI over a live, full-bleed map — search, place details, and real-time navigation — and you think in terms of what the map can carry versus what the chrome must carry.
</role>

<reference_data>
Core palette (light):
- Operating accent (route line, location dot, primary directional action): #4285F4, pressed #1A73E8, dark casing #174EA6
- Marker role A — default dropped pin: #EA4335
- Marker role B — saved/favorited pin: #34A853
- Marker role C — category pin (food, fuel, lodging, etc.): #FB8C00
- Rating/caution accent: #FBBC04
- Canvas: #FFFFFF; muted surface: #F1F3F4; hairline divider: #DADCE0
- Text primary #202124; text secondary #5F6368; text tertiary #80868B
Map tile tones (light): road #FFFFFF, highway tint #FDF6E3, water #AADAFF, park #C8E6C9, building fill #F0F0F0 with #E0E0E0 outline
Dark mode: canvas #202124, elevated surface #2D2E31, higher surface #3C4043, divider #3C4043, text primary #E8EAED, text secondary #9AA0A6; dark map tiles: land #242F3E, roads #38414E, water #17263C, parks #023E58
Type ramp (role / size / weight): in-navigation instruction 36pt/700; screen title 28pt/500; place title 20pt/500; section header 16pt/500; row title 16pt/500; body 14pt/400; meta/distance 13pt/400; tab label 11pt/500. Numerals for distance, ETA, and speed are always tabular.
Key measurements: primary circular action button 56pt diameter; pill CTA height 44pt with 22pt (full pill) radius; bottom-sheet top-corner radius 16pt with a 32×4pt grabber; floating search bar 48pt tall, full-pill radius, 16pt margin from screen edges; location dot 12pt inner circle with a 3pt white stroke and a soft accuracy halo at ~18% opacity of the accent.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Reserve the operating accent color for exactly the route line, the live-location indicator, and the single primary directional action — introducing a second UI-wide accent dilutes the "this is the one thing to tap" signal a map app depends on.
2. Give each dropped-marker color a fixed, learnable job (default result, saved place, home/work, category) rather than reusing any of them decoratively elsewhere — users build a mental taxonomy from marker color within a few sessions.
3. Never let map-tile colors and floating-UI colors overlap in hue — chrome must read as a distinct layer from the geography underneath it at a glance.
4. Keep every floating element (search bar, controls, action button) at one consistent margin from the screen edge and from each other, so the map itself stays legible as the dominant surface rather than a backdrop behind clutter.
5. Apply tabular figures to anything numeric that can update in place — distance, ETA, speed — so list rows and cards never reflow as digits change width.
6. Reserve the single largest, heaviest type moment on any screen for the most time-critical instruction visible — typically a turn direction — never for a marketing headline or a settings label.
7. Anchor markers to the map with a soft, ground-hugging elliptical shadow rather than a directional drop shadow, so pins read as resting on the world instead of floating above a card.
8. Keep camera and route-draw animations gentle (roughly a third of a second to just over half a second, eased) — anything snappier reads as a jump-cut and breaks the sense of a continuous, physical space.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: ____
Core map-based task the user completes in under ten seconds: ____
Primary accent color(s) and what each is reserved for: ____
Number and meaning of marker/pin categories needed: ____
Existing brand type faces (or "none yet"): ____
Does the app need a turn-by-turn or other real-time tracking mode? ____
Target device range (phone only / phone+tablet): ____
Light/dark mode requirement: ____
Any existing brand assets (logo, icon set) to reconcile with this system: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Token Table — every surface, text, marker, and map-tile color for light and dark, each with a one-line usage note.
2. Typography Ramp — role, face, size, weight, and line-height for every text style from the largest navigation instruction down to tab labels, flagging which sizes stay fixed under Dynamic Type.
3. Core Component Specs — the floating search bar, the primary circular map action, the bottom-sheet drawer (including its detents), and the marker/pin family, each with exact dimensions, radii, and shadow values.
4. Motion & Haptic Map — a table of every animated moment (pin drop, sheet detent change, camera recenter, live-tracking pulse) with duration, easing curve, and paired haptic if any.
5. Responsive & Touch-Target Table — behavior across the smallest supported phone through iPad, plus minimum hit-area sizing for every interactive element.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the token table, plus one fully worked signature component (the floating search bar or the marker family) as a paste-ready SwiftUI view.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Copy the promptText into a new Claude conversation or your prompt library.
Fill in the <the_project> fields for the app you're designing.
Ask for section 1 (colors) and section 2 (typography) first if you want to review the palette before generating components.
Request section 6 last so the SwiftUI code reflects any adjustments made to the tokens in earlier sections.

name: Hopper Design System
summary: iOS design reference for Hopper's price-prediction UI — the buy/wait calendar heatmap, verdict pills, and mascot-driven empty states.
description: A structured extraction of Hopper's fare-prediction visual language — its green-to-red decision heatmap, watch-price toggle, and confidence-bar pattern — for building travel apps centered on a single buy-or-wait recommendation.

whatYouGet: Full hex values for the five-stop buy→wait heatmap gradient plus the brand's semantic red/green pair
A type ramp built around one oversized predicted-price numeral paired with a compact colored verdict label
Component specs for the calendar heatmap cell, a watch/track toggle, the fare card, and a segmented confidence bar
Motion timing for heatmap color transitions, toggle arming, and a price-drop celebration moment
Explicit do/don't guidance for keeping red and green strictly semantic rather than decorative
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in decision-support consumer apps — interfaces whose entire job is to compress a probabilistic recommendation into one glanceable visual signal, the way a fare-prediction tool tells a traveler whether to buy now or wait.
</role>

<reference_data>
Heatmap scale (best-buy to worst-wait): #34C759 (best) → #A8E6B8 (good) → #F5F5F7 (neutral) → #FFC7C7 (elevated) → #FA4747 (worst)
Brand accent (primary CTA, active tab, "wait" verdict, mascot): #FA4747, pressed #E03A3A
Positive verdict / price-drop color: #34C759
Canvas #FFFFFF; grouped surface #F5F5F7; hairline divider #E5E5EA; surface-pressed #EBEBF0
Text primary #1D1D1F; text secondary #6E6E73; text tertiary #A1A1A6
Separate, non-brand error red (form validation only): #D70015
Dark mode: canvas #0F0F0F, surface #1C1C1E, text primary #FFFFFF, text secondary #A0A0A0; the heatmap and brand red/green stay identical across themes because they carry meaning, not decoration
Type ramp (role / size / weight): hero predicted price 28pt/700 with tight (-0.5pt) tracking; large screen title 28pt/700; section header 22pt/700; card/route title 17pt/700; body 15pt/400; primary button 16pt/700; verdict pill label 13pt/700 uppercase; calendar day number 14pt/600; tiny in-cell price 10pt/600; tab label 11pt/600. Weights are concentrated at 400/600/700 only — no thin or black weights anywhere.
Key measurements: primary CTA 14pt vertical / 28pt horizontal padding, 14pt corner radius; toggle track 52×32pt pill with a 28pt knob; fare card 16pt radius with a 1pt divider border; verdict pill 5pt vertical / 12pt horizontal padding at full-pill radius; calendar day cell ~44pt square with 8pt corner radius and a 4pt gap between cells.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Treat the red/green pair as a strict binary semantic — never use either color decoratively anywhere else in the interface, or the "buy versus wait" signal stops being trustworthy at a glance.
2. Keep every calendar or heatmap cell perfectly flat, with no shadow — the fill color alone must carry the signal, and adding elevation competes with that read.
3. Pair every colored verdict with an explicit short text label, never color alone, so the recommendation survives color-blindness and a black-and-white screenshot equally.
4. Give the predicted price the single largest, boldest numeral anywhere on its card — everything else (route, airline, duration) is supporting detail that recedes into gray.
5. Never let a calendar day cell shrink below a comfortably tappable size, even when compressing a full month onto the smallest supported phone — a mis-tap on a date changes the whole recommendation shown.
6. Express model confidence as a quantized segmented bar plus a stated percentage, not a vague adjective like "likely" — a user accepts the recommendation because they can see roughly how sure it is.
7. Lock any mascot or brand illustration to a single brand color across every state (empty, loading, celebration) — recoloring it dilutes recognition in exactly the moments a user most needs reassurance.
8. Reserve a separate, visually distinct error/danger red for form and validation failures so it is never confused with the "wait" verdict red, which is a friendly brand color, not a warning.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: ____
What is being predicted (price / availability / something else): ____
Wording for the positive versus negative verdict (e.g. "buy" vs. "wait"): ____
Brand accent color(s): ____
Does a mascot or illustration system already exist? ____
How should model confidence be communicated (percentage, bar, plain language)? ____
Target device range: ____
Light/dark mode requirement: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Tokens — the heatmap scale, the semantic verdict pair, and a clearly separate error/danger color, each with a usage note.
2. Typography Ramp — every text role from the hero price number down to tab labels, with size, weight, and which sizes stay fixed under Dynamic Type.
3. Signature Calendar/Heatmap Component Spec — exact cell dimensions, corner radius, color-to-value mapping, and selection state.
4. Verdict Pill & Confidence Bar Spec — dimensions, states, and how they pair with the hero price numeral.
5. Motion & Haptic Map — timing for heatmap color shifts, toggle arming, verdict pill scale-in, and a price-drop celebration.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the tokens, plus one fully worked signature component (the heatmap cell or the verdict pill) as a paste-ready view.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Copy the promptText into a new Claude conversation or your prompt library.
Fill in the <the_project> fields, being specific about what "good" versus "bad" means for your prediction.
Ask for the color tokens and heatmap spec first if you want to sanity-check the semantic scale before generating components.
Request the SwiftUI starter code last once the verdict wording and confidence presentation are settled.

name: KAYAK Design System
summary: iOS design reference for KAYAK's metasearch UI — a single scarce accent, the price-calendar strip, and a fare-compare matrix.
description: A structured extraction of KAYAK's comparison-tool visual language, covering its deliberately scarce single-brand-accent discipline, a functional price-signal ramp kept separate from that accent, and an airline-by-stops comparison matrix, for building multi-provider search and comparison apps.

whatYouGet: A palette split cleanly between one scarce brand accent and a separate functional price/forecast signal ramp
A type ramp built around mandatory tabular figures for every price, time, and comparison-matrix cell
Component specs for the fare card, the price-calendar strip, a forecast-advice banner, and an airline-by-stops comparison matrix
Motion timing for date selection, matrix-cell interaction, and result re-sorting
Explicit guidance on limiting the brand accent to one or two appearances per screen
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who builds comparison and metasearch tools — interfaces whose entire job is to let someone scan many competing options (providers, prices, schedules) at once and trust the comparison enough to act on it.
</role>

<reference_data>
Single brand accent (selected date, feature tag, primary CTA, active tab): #FF690F, pressed #E0560A, soft variant #FF8A42
Plain hyperlink color (deliberately distinct from the brand accent): #2E7CF6
Functional price-signal ramp (NOT brand colors): low/cheapest #1E9E5A, mid/typical uses primary text color, high/priciest #E5484D
Forecast-advice triad (also functional, not brand): buy #1E9E5A, wait #E8A317, book-soon/rising #E5484D
Canvas #FFFFFF, surface #F4F5F7, divider #E2E5E9; dark canvas #101214 (a near-neutral charcoal with NO brand tint), dark surface #181B1E, dark divider #2C3338
Text primary #16191C light / #E9ECEF dark; text secondary #5C656E light / #9BA3AB dark; text tertiary #8B949C light / #6B747C dark
Type ramp (role / size / weight): display 32pt/800; route/result title 26pt/800; section header 22pt/700; fare price 20pt/800 tabular; leg/segment time 18pt/800 tabular; body 16pt/400; time/label 14pt/600; meta 13pt/400; calendar-cell price 13pt/800 tabular; tag/badge 11pt/700; button 16pt/700; tab label 10pt/600. Weight is concentrated at 400/600/700/800 only.
Key measurements: primary button 14pt vertical / 28pt horizontal padding at 10pt corner radius; result card 14pt padding, 14pt corner radius, hairline border; price-calendar day cell ~50pt wide by ~58pt tall at 10pt radius; comparison-matrix container at 10pt radius with 0.5pt row dividers; feature tag 5pt radius.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Treat the single brand accent as scarce by design — no more than one or two uses of it per visible screen — so that whenever it does appear, it unambiguously means "the one important thing here."
2. Keep functional signal colors (cheap/typical/expensive pricing, buy/wait/rising forecasts) completely separate in hue from the brand accent, so a data signal is never mistaken for a brand decoration or vice versa.
3. Make every price, duration, and time figure tabular so that parallel columns in a comparison list or matrix stay visually aligned as the eye scans down them.
4. Offer a default "best" blended ranking rather than raw price alone, but always make it trivial to switch to a pure cheapest or fastest view and see the winning number for each.
5. Surface which third-party provider a price actually comes from — a comparison tool earns trust by visibly routing to a source, not by presenting itself as the merchant of record.
6. Keep comparison surfaces (calendars, matrices, forecast banners) perfectly flat with no shadow — reserve elevation for individually tappable action cards, never for a data grid.
7. Cap interactive motion under roughly 300 milliseconds using simple functional easing — a comparison tool should feel instantaneous, not showcase its transitions.
8. Never let a plain hyperlink share the brand accent color — give links their own distinct hue so the accent's scarcity, and therefore its meaning, is never diluted by routine inline text.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App/product name: ____
What exactly is being compared (providers, routes, plans, rates)? ____
Single brand accent color: ____
Separate functional signal colors needed, if any (e.g. price bands, forecast advice): ____
Default sort/ranking logic: ____
Target device range: ____
Dark-mode approach (tinted or neutral canvas)? ____
Existing type system, if any: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Tokens — the brand accent and the functional signal ramp presented as explicitly separate groups, each with a usage note.
2. Typography Ramp — every role from display down to tab labels, flagging the mandatory tabular-figure rule and which sizes stay fixed.
3. Comparison Card & Matrix Component Specs — the fare/result card and the comparison-matrix layout, with exact padding, radius, and cell states.
4. Forecast/Signal Banner Spec — layout and color-mapping for a recommendation or advice banner.
5. Motion & Interaction Timing — a table covering date selection, matrix-cell tap, and list re-sort animations.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the tokens, plus one fully worked signature component (the comparison matrix or the price-calendar strip) as a paste-ready view.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Copy the promptText into a new Claude conversation or your prompt library.
Fill in the <the_project> fields, being precise about which colors are brand versus purely functional.
Ask for the color tokens first if your team needs sign-off on the accent-versus-signal split before building components.

name: Lyft Design System
summary: iOS design reference for Lyft's map-plus-sheet UI — no tab bar, one pink accent, and a springy rounded bottom sheet.
description: A structured extraction of Lyft's ride-hailing visual language — the full-screen map with no tab navigation, a rounded bottom-sheet state machine, and its single-accent discipline — for building on-demand transportation or delivery apps.

whatYouGet: A light/dark palette built around one vivid brand accent reserved for exactly one job per screen
A type ramp tuned for a sheet-driven (not screen-driven) hierarchy, with tabular pricing figures
Component specs for the rounded bottom sheet, an option-selector row, a pickup marker, and a floating search prompt
The five-state sheet progression (idle, choose, confirm, active, rate) with its transition motion
Do/don't guidance comparing a map-plus-sheet navigation model against a conventional tab bar
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who has shipped production on-demand marketplace apps — ride-hailing, delivery, or similar — built around a live map as the primary surface, where navigation happens through map state and a sheet rather than a tab bar.
</role>

<reference_data>
Single brand accent (primary CTA, active selection, pickup marker): #FF00BF, pressed #D500A0, light tint wash #FFE5F7, dark tint wash #33102B
Light canvas #FFFFFF; surface #F4F4F7; surface-deep (pressed) #E9E9EF; divider #E5E5EA
Dark canvas #11111F; dark surface #1C1C2B; dark surface-deep #26263A; dark divider #2C2C40
Text primary #11111F light / #FFFFFF dark; text secondary #6B6B7B light / #A0A0B4 dark; text tertiary #9A9AA8
Secondary map marker (drop-off point, kept distinct from the accent): near-black #11111F
Type ramp (role / size / weight): sheet title 22pt/700; primary search prompt 20pt/600; option/item name 17pt/700; price 17pt/700 tabular, right-aligned; body 15pt/400; primary button label 17pt/700; secondary title (e.g. a matched provider's name) 18pt/700; meta/eta 14pt/400; item subtitle 13pt/400; badge 11pt/700; caption 12pt/400.
Key measurements: primary CTA 56pt tall at 16pt corner radius; bottom-sheet top corners at 28pt radius with a 36×4pt grab handle 8pt from the top; option-selector row ~72pt tall with a 2pt accent border and tinted fill when selected; floating search bar 56pt tall at 16pt radius; corner radius scale runs from 12pt (small fields) up to 28pt (the sheet itself) — nothing in the system uses a sharp corner.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Reserve the single brand accent for exactly one job per screen — the primary action, the active selection, or one key map marker — never for body text, dividers, or general decoration.
2. Drive all navigation through map state plus a bottom sheet rather than a tab bar whenever the product's core loop is a single live task (getting from A to B, or a delivery in progress) rather than browsing several unrelated sections.
3. Model the sheet as a small state machine — idle, decision, confirmation, active, completion — and let its detent height and contents change with that state, instead of routing between separate full screens.
4. Give every selectable option row (a service tier, a plan, a variant) a consistent anatomy: leading icon, name, one-line description, secondary metadata, and a right-aligned tabular price, so scanning several options stays fast.
5. Use generously rounded corners throughout — the sheet, buttons, and cards — when the brand voice is meant to read as friendly and approachable rather than clinical or utilitarian.
6. Give a marker that represents "where the user is" or "where they're going" the brand accent color, and any secondary or drop-off marker a neutral ink color, so the two are never confused on the map at a glance.
7. Build the sheet's entrance and its detent-snapping with a slight spring overshoot rather than a linear ease, so the interface feels tactile and physical rather than mechanical.
8. Support a full, first-class dark theme rather than a dimmed afterthought, since a live map product is used as often at night as during the day — and keep the brand accent at full strength in both.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: ____
Core on-demand task the user completes: ____
Single brand accent color: ____
Does the app use a full-screen live map as its primary surface? ____
The sheet/screen states the user moves through (e.g. idle → decision → confirm → active → done): ____
Target device range: ____
Dark-mode requirement: ____
Existing type system, if any: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Tokens — light and dark, with the single accent and its tint variants clearly called out.
2. Typography Ramp — every role from the sheet title down to captions, with tabular-figure rules for pricing.
3. Bottom Sheet & Option-Row Component Specs — exact corner radii, detent behavior, and the selected-state treatment for an option row.
4. Map Marker Spec — primary versus secondary marker treatment and any drop animation.
5. Sheet State Machine & Motion Timing — the states the user moves through and the spring parameters for detent changes.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the tokens, plus one fully worked signature component (the bottom sheet or the option-selector row) as a paste-ready view.
</what_to_give_me>

Ask for the bottom-sheet and option-row specs first if the map-plus-sheet model is new to your team.

name: Marriott Bonvoy Design System
summary: iOS design reference for Marriott Bonvoy's loyalty-first UI — the navy-and-gold points panel, points-aware rate cards, and keyless entry.
description: A structured extraction of Marriott Bonvoy's premium hospitality visual language — its disciplined gold-as-earned-value rule, a points-and-tier panel, and rate cards priced in both cash and points — for building loyalty-driven booking apps.

whatYouGet: A navy-and-gold palette with an explicit rule for exactly when the value accent may and may not be used
A type ramp built around an oversized points-balance numeral and letter-spaced small-caps eyebrow labels
Component specs for the points/tier panel, a points-aware rate card, a large photo hero header, and a keyless-entry card
Motion timing for a points count-up, a progress-bar fill, and rate selection
Do/don't guidance on restraint — when a premium loyalty product should deliberately withhold its accent color
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer with experience building premium loyalty and membership-driven booking products, where a disciplined "earned value" accent color has to coexist with large-format photography and never slide into decoration.
</role>

<reference_data>
Structural color, constant across light and dark (panels, secondary actions, brand frame): navy #16264A, border-on-navy #243A66, pressed navy #1F3157
Value/earned-worth accent (points, tier, redemption, primary booking action): gold #B3852A light / #D2A23E dark, pressed #8F6A1F, on-gold text #1C1206
Light canvas #FFFFFF, warm surface #F6F4EF, divider #E3E1DA; dark canvas #121214, dark surface #1A1A1D, dark divider #2E2E33
Text primary #1A1A1C light / #EDEDEF dark; text secondary #5C5C63 light / #A0A0A8 dark
Tier-accent examples: base member neutral gray; mid-tier gold-tinted pill; top-tier navy background with a gold border
Type ramp (role / size / weight): large screen title 32pt/800; points-balance numeral 26pt/800; primary item name (e.g. a property or plan name) 22pt/700; section header 18pt/700; body 16pt/400; item/rate title 15pt/600; price/rate amount 17pt/800; meta/subtitle 14pt/400; eyebrow (uppercase small-caps) 11pt/700 with roughly 1.2pt tracking; points/value-earned line 11pt/700; button 16pt/700; tab label 10pt/500.
Key measurements: primary button 14pt vertical / 28pt horizontal padding at a tight 8pt corner radius (deliberately less rounded than a typical consumer app); points/tier panel 16pt padding at 12–14pt radius with a 1pt border instead of a shadow; rate-select card 14pt padding at 10pt radius, gaining a 1pt gold border plus a light gold tint when selected; hero photo roughly 256pt tall with a bottom scrim gradient.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Reserve the value-accent color exclusively for things the member has earned or can redeem — a points balance, a tier badge, a redemption price, the primary booking action — never for generic decoration or emphasis elsewhere.
2. Give panels that represent membership status (points, tier) a bordered, inset treatment rather than a floating drop shadow, so they read as crafted and structural rather than as an ordinary elevated card.
3. Price every bookable option in both cash and loyalty currency side by side, so a member can compare either way without switching modes or opening a second screen.
4. Render sub-brand or tier names as uppercase, letter-spaced small-caps — never sentence case — to borrow the visual grammar of established hospitality wordmarks.
5. Lead every detail screen with large-format photography and let the surrounding chrome recede — the product being sold is an experience, and the interface should get out of its way.
6. Use tight, restrained corner radii rather than the generous rounding common in consumer apps, to signal premium restraint over playful friendliness.
7. Make the membership balance and tier among the most prominent, heaviest-weight type on the entire screen — loyalty is the actual product here, not a footnote in a corner.
8. Keep the structural (navy) color truly constant across light and dark modes, and only let the value accent brighten in dark mode — the brand frame should never feel like it changed identity just because the system theme did.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App/product name: ____
What the loyalty currency is and how members earn or redeem it: ____
Tier or status levels, if any: ____
Structural (non-accent) brand color(s): ____
Value/accent color reserved for earned worth: ____
Is large-format photography a primary content type? ____
Target device range: ____
Existing type system, if any: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Tokens — structural color and value accent presented as explicitly separate groups, each with a usage rule.
2. Typography Ramp — every role from the large screen title down to tab labels, including the eyebrow/small-caps treatment.
3. Membership Panel & Rate-Card Component Specs — exact padding, border treatment, and the selected/redeemed state.
4. Hero/Photography Header Spec — dimensions, scrim treatment, and overlay content layout.
5. Motion Timing — the points count-up, progress-bar fill, and rate-selection animations.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the tokens, plus one fully worked signature component (the membership panel) as a paste-ready view.
</what_to_give_me>

whatYouGet: A theme-invariant traffic-light price palette plus a single scarce brand blue reserved for actions
A type ramp emphasizing mandatory tabular figures across a price calendar, a result list, and a trend chart

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer specializing in fare and price-comparison tools, where the entire value proposition rests on making a bare numeric price instantly legible as cheap, average, or expensive.
</role>

<reference_data>
Single brand action color: #0770E3, pressed #0A5BBA, brighter dark-mode variant #05A8FA, deep brand navy #05203C
Theme-invariant price traffic light (never shifts between light/dark, because it must always mean the same thing): low/cheap #00A698, average #FFB81C, high/expensive #E5392E
Light canvas #FFFFFF, surface #F5F7FA, surface-pressed #E9EDF2, divider #E2E7EC
Dark canvas #0B0F14 (a cool navy-black, not pure black), dark surface #141A22, dark surface-2 #1C242E, dark divider #25303C
Text primary #0E1B2C light / #E8EDF2 dark; text secondary #5C6B7A light / #9AA7B4 dark; text tertiary #8B97A3 light / #66727E dark
Type ramp (role / size / weight): display 32pt/800; screen title 26pt/700; section 22pt/700; card title 18pt/700; large fare 19pt/800 tabular; body 16pt/400; inline price 15pt/600 tabular; result time 17pt/700 tabular; meta 14pt/400; airport-style code 12pt/600 uppercase; field label 12pt/600 uppercase; button 16pt/700; chip 13pt/700; tab label 10pt/600; calendar day 11pt/700 tabular; calendar micro-price 8pt/600 tabular.
Key measurements: primary button 50pt tall at 12pt corner radius, with the only persistent shadow in the whole system (a colored glow matching the accent, dropped entirely in dark mode); search/entry card 16pt radius with internal rows separated by hairline dividers and a circular swap control straddling two of those rows; price-calendar day cell roughly square with 7pt corner radius; result row 14pt corner radius with 16pt internal padding.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Encode every visible price with a fixed three-step semantic color scale (cheap / average / expensive) rather than showing a bare numeral — a price alone doesn't tell a user whether it's actually a good one.
2. Keep the semantic price-color trio completely identical between light and dark themes — its meaning must never shift just because the system appearance changed.
3. Reserve the single brand accent strictly for interactive actions — the primary button, an active tab, a selected date, a focused field — never let it double as a data-signal color, or the two meanings blur together.
4. Offer a default "best blended" sort alongside pure cheapest and fastest sorts, and make it trivial to see the winning number for whichever sort is currently active.
5. Treat an open-ended, "I don't know exactly where I'm going" search mode as a first-class, separately iconified destination option, not an edge case bolted onto a location text field.
6. Make every fare, time, and calendar figure tabular so a scanning eye can compare numbers column by column without digits changing width.
7. Give the one primary action button on a screen the only persistent shadow anywhere in the system — that shadow alone should be enough to pull the eye to the single thing worth tapping.
8. Never let a live-updating price change instantly — cross-fade or color-transition a changed number over a short duration so the update reads as new information arriving, not as a glitch.
</house_rules>

name: Southwest Airlines Design System
summary: iOS design reference for Southwest's boarding-position UI — the tri-color role system, the giant position readout, and the 24-hour check-in countdown.
description: A structured extraction of Southwest Airlines' visual language — its strict three-color role discipline for structure, action, and alerts, an oversized boarding-position display, and a launch-clock check-in countdown — for building airline or queue-position apps.

whatYouGet: A three-color brand palette with an explicit, non-negotiable role assigned to each color
A type ramp built around one extra-heavy, oversized numeral for a single time-critical readout
Component specs for a hero position/status card, a countdown-ring component, and a tiered pricing ladder
Motion timing for the "reveal" moment of a status readout and a countdown-to-deadline clock
Do/don't guidance on keeping an alert color from ever doubling as a call-to-action color
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who builds high-stakes, time-sensitive queue and status apps — interfaces where a single numeric readout, such as a position in line or a countdown to a deadline, is the entire reason someone opens the app.
</role>

<reference_data>
Three-color brand role system: structure/chrome color #304CB2 (secondary actions, headers, brand frame); action color #F9B612 (the one primary CTA, the hero readout's most prominent element), pressed #E0A300; alert-only color #E51D23 (used strictly for irregular-operation and destructive-confirm states, never decoration or a CTA)
Link/bright-blue variant (brightens for dark-mode contrast): #2567E8
Light canvas #FFFFFF, wash #F2F5FB, divider #DCE2EE; dark canvas #0E1726 (a darkened structural blue, never neutral black), dark surface #16223A, dark surface-2 #1F2E4A, dark divider #2A3A57
Text primary #1A2233 light / #EAF0FA dark; text secondary #5A6783 light / #9DAAC4 dark; text on the action-color fill uses a near-black for contrast; text on the structure-color fill uses white
Type ramp (role / size / weight): hero readout's largest element 88pt/900 with tight negative tracking; hero readout's secondary element 52pt/800; screen title 32pt/900; a short fixed-width code (e.g. an airport code) 26pt/800; section header 22pt/800; subsection 18pt/700; body 16pt/400; card title 15pt/600; tier/rate price 19pt/800 tabular; eyebrow label (uppercase, tracked) 13pt/700; meta 12pt/500; button 16pt/800; tab label 10pt/600; countdown clock 11pt (ring-mounted) or 34pt (full display), always tabular.
Key measurements: hero readout card 20pt corner radius with a soft colored-glow shadow (never a neutral gray shadow); countdown ring roughly 54pt diameter, ~5pt stroke, rounded cap, starting rotation at -90 degrees; primary button 52pt tall at a tight 8pt corner radius; tiered pricing cards at 12pt corner radius, cheapest option presented leftmost/first, with a 2pt action-color border plus a light action-color tint on the selected tier.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Assign each brand color exactly one non-negotiable role — structure, primary action, or alert — and never let a role's color perform another role's job; an alert color doubling as a call-to-action undermines the very thing it's meant to warn about.
2. Make the single most time-critical number on a given screen (a position, a countdown, a balance) the largest and heaviest-weight element on that screen, outweighing any nearby heading in both size and weight.
3. Allow only one instance of the primary-action color per screen — if two elements compete for it, the layout needs to change, not the rule.
4. Model a fixed deadline or unlock moment (a countdown to check-in, a release time) as a depleting ring or clock rather than a static label, so urgency is visually legible before anyone reads the number.
5. Use tabular, non-jittering numerals for anything that updates live — a clock, a balance, a fare — so the surrounding layout never shifts as digits change width.
6. Present a tiered set of options from cheapest or simplest first, in natural reading order, so the default scan path matches the default recommendation.
7. Keep body and label type weights heavier than a typical iOS app when the brand voice is meant to read as warm and confident rather than minimal or clinical.
8. Give the hero readout card a colored glow shadow that matches its structural brand color rather than a neutral gray shadow, so its elevation reinforces brand identity instead of looking like generic chrome.
</house_rules>

<the_project>

The single time-critical number or status the app exists to show: ____
The app's brand colors and the role each should own (structure / action / alert): ____
Is there a countdown or deadline mechanic? ____
Tiered options to present, if any (e.g. fare classes, service levels): ____
Target device range: ____
Existing type system, if any: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color Tokens — each brand color with its explicit, single assigned role and a note on where it must never appear.
2. Typography Ramp — every role from the hero readout down to tab labels, flagging which sizes stay fixed under Dynamic Type.
3. Hero Readout Card & Countdown Component Specs — exact dimensions, the glow-shadow treatment, and the countdown ring's stroke and rotation.
4. Tiered Option-Ladder Component Spec — layout, ordering, and the selected-tier treatment.
5. Motion & Haptic Timing — the reveal-moment animation and the countdown-to-deadline behavior.
6. SwiftUI Starter Code — a `Color` and `Font` extension implementing the tokens, plus one fully worked signature component (the hero readout card) as a paste-ready view.
</what_to_give_me>
